question: Will God destroy those that intermarry?
summary: Deuteronomy 7:3-4 bans intermarriage with the Canaanite nations on pain of God's anger destroying the offender "suddenly." Genesis 46:20 records Joseph's marriage to Asenath, the daughter of Potipherah, priest of the Egyptian sun-god at On/Heliopolis — a foreign priestess-daughter — with no divine pushback. The law says destruction; the narrative shows endorsement.

reconcile.connective: Defenders read Deuteronomy 7 as a targeted ban on the idolatrous Canaanite nations — admitting proselytes and falling outside Joseph's Egyptian marriage — not a blanket prohibition on all foreign unions.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells presses the objection at the source: God forbids intermarriage on pain of being "destroyed suddenly," yet Joseph married an Egyptian priest's daughter and Moses a foreign wife with no punishment — so the standard is applied inconsistently.

pd_work.note: Gill treats this passage directly, limiting the intermarriage ban to non-proselyte idolaters and noting proselyte/captive exceptions (Rahab, Ruth) — the harmonizing answer to Joseph's Egyptian marriage. Used in place of Haley because his coverage of this specific pair could not be confirmed.

link.title: GotQuestions: Who were the priests of On? Was Joseph wrong to marry the daughter of a pagan priest?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of Joseph/Asenath vs. the intermarriage prohibition: argues Joseph predated the law, married an Egyptian (not a Canaanite), and that Scripture records no condemnation.

excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Unless they became proselytes, as Rahab, who was married by Salmon, and so those of other nations, as Ruth the Moabitess, and so any captive taken in war; otherwise it was not lawful, bad consequences have followed upon it, which it is the design of this law to prevent; that is, being snared and drawn aside into idolatry, which was the case of Solomon …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly distinguishes the senses: the ban is not absolute — it admits proselytes and captives, and its purpose is to prevent idolatry, not to condemn every foreign marriage like Joseph's. NOT shipped.

Neither shalt thou make marriages with them,.... Unless they became proselytes, as Rahab, who was married by Salmon, and so those of other nations, as Ruth the Moabitess, and so any captive taken in war; otherwise it was not lawful, bad consequences have followed upon it, which it is the design of this law to prevent; that is, being snared and drawn aside into idolatry, which was the case of Solomon:
thy daughter thou shalt not give unto his son, nor his daughter shalt thou take unto thy son; for, according to the Targum of Jonathan, whosoever marries with them, it is as if he married with their idols: and this law, according to the Jewish writers (c), is binding with respect to other nations besides the seven; and whosoever marries any Heathen, of whatsoever nation, is to be beaten.
(c) Maimon. Hilchot lssure Biah, c. 12. sect. 1.
